draft.excerpt: A good garden still has something to say in January. These are the plants we lean on to keep a border looking alive through the darkest weeks.
draft.body:
January is when you find out whether a garden was designed or simply planted. Strip away the leaves and flowers, and what is left is structure: shapes, lines, bark and seed heads. If there is nothing there, the garden goes flat for three months.

We spend a lot of time on winter when we plan a garden, because in the north it lasts a long while. Here are the plants we rely on.

## Evergreen shapes

A few clipped evergreens give the eye something to rest on. They don't need to be formal. Loose domes and blocks work just as well.

- **Yew.** Slow, but nothing beats it for dense, dark green that clips to any shape.
- ***Ilex crenata*.** Our usual alternative to box, which has had a hard time with blight and caterpillar.
- ***Pittosporum tenuifolium* 'Tom Thumb'.** For a sheltered spot, a small dome of deep bronze-purple that glows in low light.

## Bark and stems

Coloured stems are the closest thing winter has to flowers.

- **Dogwoods.** *Cornus sanguinea* 'Midwinter Fire' is flame orange at the tips. Cut a third of the stems to the ground each spring to keep the colour coming.
- **Birch.** *Betula utilis* var. *jacquemontii* is the obvious choice for white bark, and obvious for a reason. Plant it where low sun will catch it.
- **Snake-bark maples.** Green and white striped bark, lovely up close.

## Seed heads and grasses

If you left your borders standing in autumn, this is your reward.

- *Phlomis russeliana* holds tiers of round brown seed heads all winter.
- *Calamagrostis* 'Karl Foerster' stays upright and pale through all but the worst storms.
- Teasels, if you let a few seed, are architecture and bird food in one.

## Scent

Winter is the season of scent, oddly. Plant these by a door or a path you use every day:

- *Sarcococca* , the Christmas box, small and glossy with a scent far bigger than it is.
- *Hamamelis* , witch hazel, with spidery yellow or copper flowers on bare branches.
- *Daphne bholua* 'Jacqueline Postill', if you can find a sheltered spot for it.

> Look at your garden from the kitchen window in January. That is the view you will see most often all winter, so plant for it.

Most of these are best planted in autumn or early spring. Make a note now, while you can see the gaps.

data.excerpt: A good garden still has something to say in January. These are the plants we lean on to keep a border looking alive through the darkest weeks.
data.body:
January is when you find out whether a garden was designed or simply planted. Strip away the leaves and flowers, and what is left is structure: shapes, lines, bark and seed heads. If there is nothing there, the garden goes flat for three months.

We spend a lot of time on winter when we plan a garden, because in the north it lasts a long while. Here are the plants we rely on.

Evergreen shapes

A few clipped evergreens give the eye something to rest on. They don't need to be formal. Loose domes and blocks work just as well.

  • Yew. Slow, but nothing beats it for dense, dark green that clips to any shape.
  • Ilex crenata. Our usual alternative to box, which has had a hard time with blight and caterpillar.
  • Pittosporum tenuifolium 'Tom Thumb'. For a sheltered spot, a small dome of deep bronze-purple that glows in low light.

Bark and stems

Coloured stems are the closest thing winter has to flowers.

  • Dogwoods. Cornus sanguinea 'Midwinter Fire' is flame orange at the tips. Cut a third of the stems to the ground each spring to keep the colour coming.
  • Birch. Betula utilis var. jacquemontii is the obvious choice for white bark, and obvious for a reason. Plant it where low sun will catch it.
  • Snake-bark maples. Green and white striped bark, lovely up close.

Seed heads and grasses

If you left your borders standing in autumn, this is your reward.

  • Phlomis russeliana holds tiers of round brown seed heads all winter.
  • Calamagrostis 'Karl Foerster' stays upright and pale through all but the worst storms.
  • Teasels, if you let a few seed, are architecture and bird food in one.

Scent

Winter is the season of scent, oddly. Plant these by a door or a path you use every day:

  • Sarcococca , the Christmas box, small and glossy with a scent far bigger than it is.
  • Hamamelis , witch hazel, with spidery yellow or copper flowers on bare branches.
  • Daphne bholua 'Jacqueline Postill', if you can find a sheltered spot for it.

Look at your garden from the kitchen window in January. That is the view you will see most often all winter, so plant for it.

Most of these are best planted in autumn or early spring. Make a note now, while you can see the gaps.

draft.title: What to do in the garden in late autumn
draft.excerpt: Less than you think. A short list of the jobs that matter in November, and a longer list of the ones you can happily leave.
draft.body:
Every November we get asked the same question by clients: what should we be doing now? The honest answer is less than you think. Late autumn is a good time to look at your garden properly, make a few careful changes and then leave it to get on with winter.

Here is how we approach it in our own gardens.

## Do these

1. **Plant trees, hedges and shrubs.** The soil is still warm, the rain has come back, and bare-root plants are cheaper and establish better than anything in a pot. If you have been meaning to put in a hedge, this is the month.
2. **Lift and divide tired perennials.** Anything that has gone bald in the middle, such as asters, hardy geraniums or sedums, can be dug up, split with two forks and replanted in smaller clumps.
3. **Mulch bare soil.** A few centimetres of compost or leaf mould on the borders keeps the soil alive over winter and saves you weeding in spring.
4. **Move anything in the wrong place.** That shrub that is too big for its corner, the grass that turned out to flop: move them now while they are slowing down.
5. **Clear leaves off lawns and paths.** Not off the borders. More on that below.

## Leave these

A tidy garden in November is often a poorer one in March. We would much rather you left:

- **Seed heads.** Teasels, grasses, rudbeckias and sedums look beautiful with frost on them, and they feed birds through the hungry months.
- **Hollow stems.** Solitary bees and other insects overwinter in them. Cut them back in spring, and leave a few short stubs even then.
- **Leaves in the borders.** They rot down where they fall and do the same job as the mulch you would otherwise buy.
- **Tender plants.** If dahlias and salvias have survived the first frost, they are better left with a thick mulch over their crowns than lifted and stored badly.

## A note on bonfires

Please don't. Hedgehogs look for exactly the sort of loose, dry pile you have just made, and smoke is no fun for the neighbours. Shred what you can, compost the rest, and take woody waste to the tip.

> The best thing you can do in late autumn is put the kettle on and look out of the window for a while.

That is not a joke. Notice where the low sun falls, where water sits after rain, which corners still look good and which look empty. Write it down. Those notes will be more useful in January, when you are planning, than anything you could do with a rake today.

examples.title: Our first apprentice
examples.excerpt: Northfold is taking on its first apprentice in January. Two years on site and in the studio, no degree needed, and applications close on 30 November.
examples.body:
We're taking on an apprentice. It's the first time Northfold has done this, it starts in January, and it runs for two years. You don't need a degree, just a real wish to get into garden design and landscaping. Letters need to reach us by 30 November.

We've never done this before. We're rather looking forward to it.

## What the two years involve

You'll split your time between site and the design office. On site, that's the real work of making a garden: digging the soil pit we dig on every project, setting out beds, planting, and going back later to see what has thrived and what has sulked. In the office, it's surveys, drawings and planting plans, and we start those by hand before anything goes near a screen.

You'll learn by doing, alongside the rest of us, on real gardens for real people.

## Who we're looking for

Someone curious and practical. You don't need a degree. You might be leaving school. You might be changing career. You might be the person friends ring when their roses look poorly, who has never quite had the chance to do it properly.

What matters is that you notice things, ask why, and don't mind muddy knees. Most of our gardens are in Northumberland, so you'll need to be local, or happy to become so.

## How to apply

There's no form. Just write us a short letter about one thing:

**A garden or landscape you love, and why.**

It can be famous, or it can be your gran's back yard. A page is plenty. We'd much rather hear what you noticed than read a list of what you've done.

Send it to the studio by **30 November**. If you have questions before then, get in touch. We're happy to chat.

And if someone you know should read this, please pass it on.

We don't know yet who will write to us, or which garden they'll choose. That's the part we're most looking forward to. Will we do it again? Ask us in two years.

examples.title: A walled garden in Corbridge, two years on
examples.excerpt: We went back to a walled garden we planted in 2024 to see what had worked, what had sulked and what the owners had quietly moved.
examples.body:
Two summers ago we finished planting a walled kitchen garden on the edge of Corbridge. Last week we went back with a flask of coffee and a notebook, because the only honest way to learn whether a garden works is to see it after the people who made it have gone home.

The short answer is that it works. The longer answer is more useful, so here it is.

## What we were asked for

The owners, Ruth and Simon, had inherited a walled garden that had been grassed over in the 1970s. The brick was sound, the gate was not, and there was a pear tree in the north-west corner that nobody could put a name to. They wanted somewhere to grow food, somewhere to sit out of the wind, and a garden that would still look cared for in the weeks when they were too busy to care for it.

That last point shaped everything. A kitchen garden can look wonderful in August and miserable in February, and we wanted this one to hold its shape all year.

## What we did

- Split the space into four beds with a cross of gravel paths, wide enough for a wheelbarrow and two people walking side by side.
- Edged every bed in low box alternatives (we used *Ilex crenata* ) so the pattern reads even when the beds are bare.
- Planted the warm south-facing wall with trained fruit: two apricots, a fig and a run of espalier pears.
- Put a deep perennial border along the inside of the east wall, for flowers to cut and for the bees.
- Built a simple oak bench into the sunniest corner, out of the draught from the gate.

## What we found

The structure has done its job. Even in a dry late summer, with half the vegetable beds cleared, the garden looked deliberate rather than abandoned. The hedging has knitted together and the paths have settled into a pleasant, crunchy grey.

The fruit wall is the star. The fig has fruited both years, which surprised all of us this far north, and the pears are already filling their wires.

Not everything has thrived. The salvias we chose for the border have struggled in the heavy soil along the east wall, and Ruth has replaced most of them with hardy geraniums from a friend's garden. She was slightly apologetic about this. She needn't have been. A garden that its owners feel free to change is a garden that is being used, and that is the point.

> We thought we'd be precious about it. Instead we're out there every evening, moving things around and eating the evidence. – Ruth

## What we'd do differently

We would dig more organic matter into the east border before planting, and we would have trusted our first instinct about the gate. We kept the old one and repaired it. It has already needed repairing again.

If you have a walled garden, or a space you'd like to feel like one, we would love to hear about it.

draft.title: A school garden in Prudhoe
draft.excerpt: We spent a year designing and building a garden with, not just for, the children of a primary school in Prudhoe. They were tough clients.
draft.body:
Last autumn a primary school in Prudhoe asked whether we could help them turn a strip of rough grass beside the playground into a garden. They had a little money from a local trust, a lot of enthusiasm and one very determined head teacher.

We said yes on the condition that the children designed it with us. It was the best decision we made all year.

## Designing with children

We ran three sessions with each class, from Reception to Year 6. We walked the site, measured it with string and pacing, and talked about what gardens are for. Then we asked them to draw what they wanted.

We got a lot of drawings. Among the most common requests:

- Somewhere to hide.
- Things to eat, preferably strawberries.
- A path that goes round in a circle so you can run.
- Animals. Specifically, in one case, a horse.

We couldn't do the horse. We did everything else.

## What we built

The garden is laid out around a looping bark path, wide enough for two children to pass. Inside the loop are six raised beds, one for each year group, at heights that suit small arms. Around the outside is a mixed native hedge, with a willow tunnel at one end that has become, as requested, the place to hide.

There is a small wildlife pond, safely fenced, a bug hotel the Year 4s built from pallets, and a strawberry bed which has been, frankly, a victim of its own success.

## The planting

Hannah led on the planting, and she chose for touch and smell as much as for looks. There is lamb's ear to stroke, rosemary and mint to crush, and sunflowers that the Year 1s measure themselves against every September. Nearly everything is tough, cheap and easy to propagate, so the school can replace losses for free.

> The children walk differently in there. They slow down. – Mrs Ellison, head teacher

## A year on

The garden is used every day. There is a gardening club on Thursdays, the Reception class does story time in the willow tunnel, and the kitchen has started using the herbs. The plants from our show garden in Harrogate have filled out a new border by the gate.

If you are part of a school or community group with a patch of ground and an idea, please get in touch. We keep a little time each year for projects like this one.

data.title: A school garden in Prudhoe
data.excerpt: We spent a year designing and building a garden with, not just for, the children of a primary school in Prudhoe. They were tough clients.
data.body:
Last autumn a primary school in Prudhoe asked whether we could help them turn a strip of rough grass beside the playground into a garden. They had a little money from a local trust, a lot of enthusiasm and one very determined head teacher.

We said yes on the condition that the children designed it with us. It was the best decision we made all year.

Designing with children

We ran three sessions with each class, from Reception to Year 6. We walked the site, measured it with string and pacing, and talked about what gardens are for. Then we asked them to draw what they wanted.

We got a lot of drawings. Among the most common requests:

  • Somewhere to hide.
  • Things to eat, preferably strawberries.
  • A path that goes round in a circle so you can run.
  • Animals. Specifically, in one case, a horse.

We couldn't do the horse. We did everything else.

What we built

The garden is laid out around a looping bark path, wide enough for two children to pass. Inside the loop are six raised beds, one for each year group, at heights that suit small arms. Around the outside is a mixed native hedge, with a willow tunnel at one end that has become, as requested, the place to hide.

There is a small wildlife pond, safely fenced, a bug hotel the Year 4s built from pallets, and a strawberry bed which has been, frankly, a victim of its own success.

The planting

Hannah led on the planting, and she chose for touch and smell as much as for looks. There is lamb's ear to stroke, rosemary and mint to crush, and sunflowers that the Year 1s measure themselves against every September. Nearly everything is tough, cheap and easy to propagate, so the school can replace losses for free.

The children walk differently in there. They slow down. – Mrs Ellison, head teacher

A year on

The garden is used every day. There is a gardening club on Thursdays, the Reception class does story time in the willow tunnel, and the kitchen has started using the herbs. The plants from our show garden in Harrogate have filled out a new border by the gate.

If you are part of a school or community group with a patch of ground and an idea, please get in touch. We keep a little time each year for projects like this one.

examples.title: A walled garden in Corbridge, two years on
examples.excerpt: We went back to a walled garden we planted in 2024 to see what had worked, what had sulked and what the owners had quietly moved.
examples.body:
Two summers ago we finished planting a walled kitchen garden on the edge of Corbridge. Last week we went back with a flask of coffee and a notebook, because the only honest way to learn whether a garden works is to see it after the people who made it have gone home.

The short answer is that it works. The longer answer is more useful, so here it is.

## What we were asked for

The owners, Ruth and Simon, had inherited a walled garden that had been grassed over in the 1970s. The brick was sound, the gate was not, and there was a pear tree in the north-west corner that nobody could put a name to. They wanted somewhere to grow food, somewhere to sit out of the wind, and a garden that would still look cared for in the weeks when they were too busy to care for it.

That last point shaped everything. A kitchen garden can look wonderful in August and miserable in February, and we wanted this one to hold its shape all year.

## What we did

- Split the space into four beds with a cross of gravel paths, wide enough for a wheelbarrow and two people walking side by side.
- Edged every bed in low box alternatives (we used *Ilex crenata* ) so the pattern reads even when the beds are bare.
- Planted the warm south-facing wall with trained fruit: two apricots, a fig and a run of espalier pears.
- Put a deep perennial border along the inside of the east wall, for flowers to cut and for the bees.
- Built a simple oak bench into the sunniest corner, out of the draught from the gate.

## What we found

The structure has done its job. Even in a dry late summer, with half the vegetable beds cleared, the garden looked deliberate rather than abandoned. The hedging has knitted together and the paths have settled into a pleasant, crunchy grey.

The fruit wall is the star. The fig has fruited both years, which surprised all of us this far north, and the pears are already filling their wires.

Not everything has thrived. The salvias we chose for the border have struggled in the heavy soil along the east wall, and Ruth has replaced most of them with hardy geraniums from a friend's garden. She was slightly apologetic about this. She needn't have been. A garden that its owners feel free to change is a garden that is being used, and that is the point.

> We thought we'd be precious about it. Instead we're out there every evening, moving things around and eating the evidence. – Ruth

## What we'd do differently

We would dig more organic matter into the east border before planting, and we would have trusted our first instinct about the gate. We kept the old one and repaired it. It has already needed repairing again.

If you have a walled garden, or a space you'd like to feel like one, we would love to hear about it.

draft.title: Why we start every project with a soil pit
draft.excerpt: Before we draw a single line, we dig a hole. It is the cheapest and most useful hour of any project.
draft.body:
Clients are sometimes surprised that our first visit involves a spade. They have been expecting sketches, mood boards, perhaps a conversation about colour. Instead, one of us disappears into a corner of the garden and comes back twenty minutes later with muddy knees and a lot of opinions.

We dig a soil pit on every project, however small. Here is why.

## The soil decides what will grow

Every planting plan is a bet on the ground underneath it. Plants that love free-draining, poor soil will rot in wet clay. Plants that need moisture will scorch on sand. You can improve soil, but only so far and only so fast, and it is far better to choose plants that will be happy where they are than to fight the ground for years.

A soil test kit tells you about pH. A pit tells you about everything else.

## What we look for

We dig down about 60 centimetres, keep the sides clean and look at the profile. In particular:

- **Depth of topsoil.** The dark, crumbly layer at the top. In new-build gardens it can be a thin skin over builder's rubble.
- **Texture.** We rub a moist pinch between finger and thumb. Gritty means sand, silky means silt, sticky means clay.
- **Colour and mottling.** Grey or blue-grey patches with orange streaks mean the ground sits wet for long periods.
- **Compaction.** A hard layer that the spade bounces off, often where machinery has driven.
- **Life.** Worms, roots, the smell of it. Healthy soil smells sweet and earthy. Sour soil smells of eggs.

Then we fill the pit with water and come back later to see how fast it drains.

## What it changes

On a project in Hexham last year, the pit showed a hard pan at about 30 centimetres, left by the diggers that built the house. Above it the soil was fine. Below it, water had nowhere to go. Breaking up that one layer before planting did more for the garden than any amount of compost would have.

On another, in a cottage garden near Bellingham, the pit told us the opposite: deep, dark, wonderful loam, improved by a century of vegetable growing. We changed the whole plan to make the most of it.

> We have never regretted digging a pit. We have regretted not digging one.

## Try it yourself

You don't need us to do this. Pick a spot in the middle of a border, dig straight down, and look. Take a photo. Fill it with water and time how long it takes to drain. If it is still full the next morning, you have learned something important about your garden, and it cost you nothing but an hour.

draft.title: The courtyard at Allendale Mill
draft.excerpt: A shady stone courtyard between a converted mill and its old workshops, planted for ferns, moss and the sound of running water.
draft.body:
Some sites tell you exactly what they want to be. The courtyard at Allendale Mill was one of them.

It sits between the converted mill building and a row of old workshops, now holiday cottages. It is enclosed on three sides by high stone walls, it gets about two hours of direct sun in midsummer and none at all from October to March, and there is a mill race running underneath it. When we first visited, it was a car park.

## The brief

The owners wanted a shared space for guests that felt calm and green, could be enjoyed in any weather, and would cope with a lot of feet. They also wanted to stop people parking in it, which, as anyone who has tried will know, is a design problem in itself.

## Working with the shade

We didn't try to brighten the courtyard. We leaned into what it already was: cool, damp and sheltered.

- The tarmac came up and was replaced with reclaimed sandstone setts, laid with wide joints so moss can creep in.
- Four large raised beds, built from the same stone, hold the planting and break up the space so it can't be parked in.
- The planting is mostly ferns, with hellebores, epimediums, woodrush and a carpet of *Asarum* underneath. There is very little colour and nobody misses it.
- Three multi-stemmed snake-bark maples give height without casting more shade than the walls already do.

## The rill

The best idea on the project wasn't ours. The site manager, Peter, mentioned on our second visit that you could hear the mill race running underneath the car park if you stood in the right place.

So we brought a little of it up. A narrow stone rill now runs the length of the courtyard, fed by a small pump from the race and returning to it at the far end. It is only fifteen centimetres wide. You can step over it without noticing. But you can hear it from every bench, and on a still evening it fills the whole space.

> Guests ask us what we did to make it so quiet. We tell them we added some noise. – Peter, site manager

## Two years later

The ferns have filled out, the moss has found the joints between the setts exactly as we hoped, and nobody has parked in it since. It is the sort of project we would like to do more of: a hard, overlooked space, turned into somewhere people choose to sit.

examples.title: Our first apprentice
examples.excerpt: Northfold is taking on its first apprentice in January. Two years on site and in the studio, no degree needed, and applications close on 30 November.
examples.body:
We're taking on an apprentice. It's the first time Northfold has done this, it starts in January, and it runs for two years. You don't need a degree, just a real wish to get into garden design and landscaping. Letters need to reach us by 30 November.

We've never done this before. We're rather looking forward to it.

## What the two years involve

You'll split your time between site and the design office. On site, that's the real work of making a garden: digging the soil pit we dig on every project, setting out beds, planting, and going back later to see what has thrived and what has sulked. In the office, it's surveys, drawings and planting plans, and we start those by hand before anything goes near a screen.

You'll learn by doing, alongside the rest of us, on real gardens for real people.

## Who we're looking for

Someone curious and practical. You don't need a degree. You might be leaving school. You might be changing career. You might be the person friends ring when their roses look poorly, who has never quite had the chance to do it properly.

What matters is that you notice things, ask why, and don't mind muddy knees. Most of our gardens are in Northumberland, so you'll need to be local, or happy to become so.

## How to apply

There's no form. Just write us a short letter about one thing:

**A garden or landscape you love, and why.**

It can be famous, or it can be your gran's back yard. A page is plenty. We'd much rather hear what you noticed than read a list of what you've done.

Send it to the studio by **30 November**. If you have questions before then, get in touch. We're happy to chat.

And if someone you know should read this, please pass it on.

We don't know yet who will write to us, or which garden they'll choose. That's the part we're most looking forward to. Will we do it again? Ask us in two years.

examples.title: A walled garden in Corbridge, two years on
examples.excerpt: We went back to a walled garden we planted in 2024 to see what had worked, what had sulked and what the owners had quietly moved.
examples.body:
Two summers ago we finished planting a walled kitchen garden on the edge of Corbridge. Last week we went back with a flask of coffee and a notebook, because the only honest way to learn whether a garden works is to see it after the people who made it have gone home.

The short answer is that it works. The longer answer is more useful, so here it is.

## What we were asked for

The owners, Ruth and Simon, had inherited a walled garden that had been grassed over in the 1970s. The brick was sound, the gate was not, and there was a pear tree in the north-west corner that nobody could put a name to. They wanted somewhere to grow food, somewhere to sit out of the wind, and a garden that would still look cared for in the weeks when they were too busy to care for it.

That last point shaped everything. A kitchen garden can look wonderful in August and miserable in February, and we wanted this one to hold its shape all year.

## What we did

- Split the space into four beds with a cross of gravel paths, wide enough for a wheelbarrow and two people walking side by side.
- Edged every bed in low box alternatives (we used *Ilex crenata* ) so the pattern reads even when the beds are bare.
- Planted the warm south-facing wall with trained fruit: two apricots, a fig and a run of espalier pears.
- Put a deep perennial border along the inside of the east wall, for flowers to cut and for the bees.
- Built a simple oak bench into the sunniest corner, out of the draught from the gate.

## What we found

The structure has done its job. Even in a dry late summer, with half the vegetable beds cleared, the garden looked deliberate rather than abandoned. The hedging has knitted together and the paths have settled into a pleasant, crunchy grey.

The fruit wall is the star. The fig has fruited both years, which surprised all of us this far north, and the pears are already filling their wires.

Not everything has thrived. The salvias we chose for the border have struggled in the heavy soil along the east wall, and Ruth has replaced most of them with hardy geraniums from a friend's garden. She was slightly apologetic about this. She needn't have been. A garden that its owners feel free to change is a garden that is being used, and that is the point.

> We thought we'd be precious about it. Instead we're out there every evening, moving things around and eating the evidence. – Ruth

## What we'd do differently

We would dig more organic matter into the east border before planting, and we would have trusted our first instinct about the gate. We kept the old one and repaired it. It has already needed repairing again.

If you have a walled garden, or a space you'd like to feel like one, we would love to hear about it.

draft.title: Rain gardens for ordinary front gardens
draft.excerpt: A rain garden catches water from a roof or a drive and lets it soak away slowly. They are simple, cheap and suit almost any front garden.
draft.body:
Summer storms are getting heavier. When a lot of rain falls in a short time onto roofs, drives and paved front gardens, it rushes straight into drains that were never built for it. Streets flood. Rivers spike. Sewers overflow.

A rain garden is a small, practical answer to that, and you can make one in an afternoon.

## What it is

A rain garden is a shallow planted dip that collects water running off a hard surface and lets it soak into the ground slowly, over a day or so, instead of all at once. It is not a pond. It should be dry most of the time, and it should never hold standing water for more than about 48 hours.

## How to make one

1. **Find the water.** Watch where it goes in heavy rain. A downpipe is the easiest source: you can disconnect it from the drain and send it across the garden in a short channel or pipe.
2. **Pick a spot.** At least a couple of metres from the house, and not over a soakaway or a septic tank. A low point is good, as long as water does drain away there eventually.
3. **Test the drainage.** Dig a hole about 30 centimetres deep, fill it with water and see how long it takes to empty. If it is still full the next day, your rain garden needs to be bigger and shallower, or somewhere else.
4. **Dig a shallow basin.** Ten to twenty centimetres deep is usually plenty, with gently sloping sides. Use the soil you dig out to make a low lip on the downhill side.
5. **Plant it.** Then mulch.

## What to plant

Rain garden plants have a tough job. They need to cope with being waterlogged for a day and bone dry for a fortnight. These do well for us:

- In the wettest middle: *Iris sibirica* , *Carex* , purple loosestrife, meadowsweet.
- On the sides: hardy geraniums, *Persicaria* , astrantia, and ferns in shade.
- On the drier rim: grasses such as *Deschampsia* , and anything you would plant in an ordinary border.

> A rain garden does its best work in the worst weather, which is when you are least likely to be looking at it.

## Is it worth it?

One small rain garden won't stop a street flooding. But it will hold back a surprising amount of water from a single roof, and it makes a better front garden than another square of gravel. If every house on a street had one, it would make a real difference.

We have designed rain gardens for houses, schools and a car park. If you'd like help planning one, get in touch.

On site, that's the real work of making a garden: digging the soil pit we dig on every project, setting out beds, planting, and going back later to see what has thrived and what has sulked. In the office, it's surveys, drawings and planting plans, and we start those by hand before anything goes near a screen.

You'll learn by doing, alongside the rest of us, on real gardens for real people.

## Who we're looking for

Someone curious and practical. You don't need a degree. You might be leaving school. You might be changing career. You might be the person friends ring when their roses look poorly, who has never quite had the chance to do it properly.

What matters is that you notice things, ask why, and don't mind muddy knees. Most of our gardens are in Northumberland, so you'll need to be local, or happy to become so.

## How to apply

There's no form. Just write us a short letter about one thing:

**A garden or landscape you love, and why.**

It can be famous, or it can be your gran's back yard. A page is plenty. We'd much rather hear what you noticed than read a list of what you've done.

Send it to the studio by **30 November**. If you have questions before then, get in touch. We're happy to chat.

And if someone you know should read this, please pass it on.

We don't know yet who will write to us, or which garden they'll choose. That's the part we're most looking forward to. Will we do it again? Ask us in two years.

examples.title: A walled garden in Corbridge, two years on
examples.excerpt: We went back to a walled garden we planted in 2024 to see what had worked, what had sulked and what the owners had quietly moved.
examples.body:
Two summers ago we finished planting a walled kitchen garden on the edge of Corbridge. Last week we went back with a flask of coffee and a notebook, because the only honest way to learn whether a garden works is to see it after the people who made it have gone home.

The short answer is that it works. The longer answer is more useful, so here it is.

## What we were asked for

The owners, Ruth and Simon, had inherited a walled garden that had been grassed over in the 1970s. The brick was sound, the gate was not, and there was a pear tree in the north-west corner that nobody could put a name to. They wanted somewhere to grow food, somewhere to sit out of the wind, and a garden that would still look cared for in the weeks when they were too busy to care for it.

That last point shaped everything. A kitchen garden can look wonderful in August and miserable in February, and we wanted this one to hold its shape all year.

## What we did

- Split the space into four beds with a cross of gravel paths, wide enough for a wheelbarrow and two people walking side by side.
- Edged every bed in low box alternatives (we used *Ilex crenata* ) so the pattern reads even when the beds are bare.
- Planted the warm south-facing wall with trained fruit: two apricots, a fig and a run of espalier pears.
- Put a deep perennial border along the inside of the east wall, for flowers to cut and for the bees.
- Built a simple oak bench into the sunniest corner, out of the draught from the gate.

## What we found

The structure has done its job. Even in a dry late summer, with half the vegetable beds cleared, the garden looked deliberate rather than abandoned. The hedging has knitted together and the paths have settled into a pleasant, crunchy grey.

The fruit wall is the star. The fig has fruited both years, which surprised all of us this far north, and the pears are already filling their wires.

Not everything has thrived. The salvias we chose for the border have struggled in the heavy soil along the east wall, and Ruth has replaced most of them with hardy geraniums from a friend's garden. She was slightly apologetic about this. She needn't have been. A garden that its owners feel free to change is a garden that is being used, and that is the point.

> We thought we'd be precious about it. Instead we're out there every evening, moving things around and eating the evidence. – Ruth

## What we'd do differently

We would dig more organic matter into the east border before planting, and we would have trusted our first instinct about the gate. We kept the old one and repaired it. It has already needed repairing again.

If you have a walled garden, or a space you'd like to feel like one, we would love to hear about it.

data.title: Rain gardens for ordinary front gardens
data.excerpt: A rain garden catches water from a roof or a drive and lets it soak away slowly. They are simple, cheap and suit almost any front garden.
data.body:
Summer storms are getting heavier. When a lot of rain falls in a short time onto roofs, drives and paved front gardens, it rushes straight into drains that were never built for it. Streets flood. Rivers spike. Sewers overflow.

A rain garden is a small, practical answer to that, and you can make one in an afternoon.

What it is

A rain garden is a shallow planted dip that collects water running off a hard surface and lets it soak into the ground slowly, over a day or so, instead of all at once. It is not a pond. It should be dry most of the time, and it should never hold standing water for more than about 48 hours.

How to make one

  1. Find the water. Watch where it goes in heavy rain. A downpipe is the easiest source: you can disconnect it from the drain and send it across the garden in a short channel or pipe.
  2. Pick a spot. At least a couple of metres from the house, and not over a soakaway or a septic tank. A low point is good, as long as water does drain away there eventually.
  3. Test the drainage. Dig a hole about 30 centimetres deep, fill it with water and see how long it takes to empty. If it is still full the next day, your rain garden needs to be bigger and shallower, or somewhere else.
  4. Dig a shallow basin. Ten to twenty centimetres deep is usually plenty, with gently sloping sides. Use the soil you dig out to make a low lip on the downhill side.
  5. Plant it. Then mulch.

What to plant

Rain garden plants have a tough job. They need to cope with being waterlogged for a day and bone dry for a fortnight. These do well for us:

  • In the wettest middle: Iris sibirica , Carex , purple loosestrife, meadowsweet.
  • On the sides: hardy geraniums, Persicaria , astrantia, and ferns in shade.
  • On the drier rim: grasses such as Deschampsia , and anything you would plant in an ordinary border.

A rain garden does its best work in the worst weather, which is when you are least likely to be looking at it.

Is it worth it?

One small rain garden won't stop a street flooding. But it will hold back a surprising amount of water from a single roof, and it makes a better front garden than another square of gravel. If every house on a street had one, it would make a real difference.
